rows.citation: Ludwig O, Anklesaria N, Jin Z, et al. (2026). Kaizen: Metamorphic Fuzzing and Differential Testing for LLM-Translated HPC Applications. arXiv:2607.04058 [cs.SE] (preprint; comments state under review at ACM TOSEM).
rows.model_type: general HPC scientific applications (CUDA-to-OpenMP translation of 16 HeCBench apps; motivating example is a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron kernel)
rows.controlled_mutations: partial - 15 grammar-based source mutation operators, but they create semantics-preserving program variants to diversify translation inputs, not single-fault mutants.
rows.multiple_stimuli: partial - grammar-based runtime input fuzzing (boundary, random, mutation-based, coverage-guided) over dimensions, parameters and data arrays; not electrophysiological stimuli.
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - outputs compared with configurable error norms or each app's built-in check; LIF example compares spike values, no electrophysiology feature extraction.
rows.protocol_optimization: partial - coverage-guided prioritization of fuzzed inputs; no budgeted selection of a compact test battery.
rows.heldout_evaluation: partial - full-program translation prompt engineered on 5 held-out HeCBench apps; no held-out models or fault families for a selected test set.
rows.ai_transformations: yes - core subject: three fine-tuned LLMs translating CUDA to OpenMP at kernel and full-program granularity.
rows.software: Kaizen replication package, https://github.com/ANSWER-OSU/Kaizen-Replication-Package (GitHub API reports no license)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Anticipates NeuroSem's motivation (code passes developer tests yet gives wrong scientific output) for LLM-translated HPC code. NeuroSem would instead target NeuroML/LEMS neuron models with electrophysiology protocols and features, refinement-calibrated tolerances, deliberate single-fault mutants, greedy budgeted protocol selection and held-out model/mutation-family evaluation.
rows.verification_method: arXiv abstract page citation meta tags and submission history (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.04058, v1 4 Jul 2026); arXiv HTML full text sections 3-5 and threats (https://arxiv.org/html/2607.04058); GitHub REST API for replication repo (https://api.github.com/repos/ANSWER-OSU/Kaizen-Replication-Package). arXiv export API returned 503.

rows.citation: Li M, Yang X, Liu J, et al. (2026). A semantic mutation metric for metamorphic relation adequacy in scientific computing programs. arXiv:2605.17437 [cs.SE] (preprint, v2).
rows.model_type: general scientific computing programs (12 single-output float-to-float Python programs: numeric incl. Lorenz ODE and 1D heat PDE, probabilistic, surrogate, ML)
rows.controlled_mutations: yes - five domain-semantic mutation operator classes; LLM-generated mutant pools with lint, self-test and reviewer prescreen; equivalent mutants excluded from the score denominator.
rows.multiple_stimuli: partial - metamorphic relations checked over sampled inputs, including an out-of-distribution band; no stimulation protocols.
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - scalar float outputs checked via metamorphic relations and statistical comparisons; no neuronal features.
rows.protocol_optimization: no - defines an adequacy score and MR coverage matrix for relation sets; no budgeted test-subset selection found in the sections read.
rows.heldout_evaluation: no - pre-registered hypotheses and bootstrap power analysis, but no held-out programs or held-out operator family reported.
rows.ai_transformations: partial - LLMs generate and review the mutants; AI-edited code is the fault source, not an evaluated real-world transformation task.
rows.software: Replication package cited in the paper as Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20250664, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20250664 (Zenodo record not fetched; license unverified)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Overlaps on domain-specific mutation operators, equivalent-mutant exclusion and separating tolerance artefacts from true kills (via replicate fail ratios). NeuroSem differs by targeting NeuroML neuron models, calibrating tolerances by time-step refinement, using electrophysiology protocols/features, and selecting protocol batteries evaluated on held-out models and families.
rows.verification_method: arXiv abstract page citation meta tags and submission history (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17437, v1 17 May 2026, v2 7 Jul 2026); arXiv HTML full text sections 4.1, 4.10, 4.11 (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.17437).

rows.citation: Yale University & Blue Brain Project/EPFL (2021). nrn-modeldb-ci: NEURON ModelDB CI tools. GitHub repository neuronsimulator/nrn-modeldb-ci; PyPI package nrn-modeldb-ci.
rows.model_type: published NEURON (HOC/NMODL) models retrieved from ModelDB (NEURON-tagged entries), run across two NEURON versions
rows.controlled_mutations: no - reruns unmodified published models under two NEURON versions; no seeded faults.
rows.multiple_stimuli: no - each model runs its own mosinit or configured run instructions; no systematic stimulus battery.
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - diffs raw graph output (gout), stdout and model errors, with regex curation of noisy lines; no extracted features.
rows.protocol_optimization: no - no selection of tests; PR runs use a default or user-specified model subset.
rows.heldout_evaluation: no - operational continuous-integration tool, not an experimental evaluation.
rows.software: nrn-modeldb-ci, https://github.com/neuronsimulator/nrn-modeldb-ci (BSD-3-Clause per GitHub API and LICENSE.txt; PyPI version 0.3.0)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Already does large-scale regression testing of hundreds of published neuron models across simulator versions using each model's single built-in run, so NeuroSem must not claim novelty for simulator-version regression. NeuroSem would add model-file edits and mutants, multi-protocol stimuli, feature-level refinement-calibrated tolerances and protocol selection.
rows.verification_method: GitHub REST API (https://api.github.com/repos/neuronsimulator/nrn-modeldb-ci: created 2021-11-05, pushed 2026-09-05, BSD-3-Clause); raw README.md and LICENSE.txt; modeldb/modeldb-run.yaml excerpt; PyPI JSON API (https://pypi.org/pypi/nrn-modeldb-ci/json).

rows.citation: CSCS & Forschungszentrum Juelich (arbor-sim) (2018). NSuite: a framework for benchmarks and numerical validation of multi-compartment neural network simulators. GitHub repository arbor-sim/nsuite.
rows.model_type: simulator validation models (rallpack1, cable steady-state, RC cells with exponential synapses) for Arbor, NEURON and CoreNEURON
rows.controlled_mutations: no - validates simulator engines against reference solutions; no model mutants.
rows.multiple_stimuli: partial - each of four validation models may have several parameter sets; not an electrophysiology stimulus battery.
rows.electrophysiology_features: no - compares NetCDF variables with (interpolated) references via absolute/relative errors and threshold predicates.
rows.heldout_evaluation: no - benchmark and validation framework, no held-out design.
rows.software: NSuite, https://github.com/arbor-sim/nsuite; docs https://nsuite.readthedocs.io (LICENSE text BSD-3-style; GitHub SPDX NOASSERTION; last push 2024-04-26)
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Targets simulator-engine correctness and performance regressions with thresholded comparison to reference solutions, including interpolation-error bounds. NeuroSem targets behavioural changes from edits to NeuroML model files, adding mutants, stimulus protocols, eFEL features, refinement-derived tolerances and protocol selection. GitHub description also names NEST, while docs list Arbor, NEURON, CoreNEURON.
rows.verification_method: GitHub REST API (https://api.github.com/repos/arbor-sim/nsuite: created 2018-06-11, license NOASSERTION); raw LICENSE, readme.md, docs/index.rst and docs/validation.rst; contents API for validation/ directory.

rows.citation: DeMillo RA, Lipton RJ, Sayward FG (1978). Hints on Test Data Selection: Help for the Practicing Programmer. Computer 11(4):34-41.
rows.controlled_mutations: partial - abstract argues tests exposing simple errors often expose complex ones (coupling effect); full text not accessed to confirm method details.
rows.multiple_stimuli: unclear - concerns test data selection generally; full text not accessed.
rows.protocol_optimization: unclear - about choosing test data, but selection method not verified (closed full text).
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Foundational background for using simple seeded faults as proxies (coupling effect). NeuroSem inherits this rationale for single-fault mutants but applies it to neuron models; cite as background, not a competing method.
rows.verification_method: Crossref API (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1109/c-m.1978.218136: title, authors, Computer vol 11 issue 4 pp 34-41, April 1978); OpenAlex abstract (https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1109/c-m.1978.218136); Semantic Scholar API cross-check.

rows.citation: Just R, Jalali D, Inozemtseva L, et al. (2014). Are mutants a valid substitute for real faults in software testing? Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE 2014), pp. 654-665.
rows.model_type: general software (5 open-source applications, about 321k lines of code)
rows.controlled_mutations: yes - systematically seeded mutants compared with 357 real developer-fixed faults.
rows.multiple_stimuli: partial - uses developer-written and automatically generated test suites; no stimulation protocols.
rows.protocol_optimization: no - correlational study of mutant versus real-fault detection, not test-suite selection.
rows.heldout_evaluation: no - validates mutants against real faults, controlling for coverage; no held-out split.
rows.distinction_from_neurosem: Gives general-software evidence that mutant detection correlates with real-fault detection, independent of coverage. That evidence may not transfer to neuron models, so NeuroSem needs its own external-validity argument, e.g. valid-transformation controls and realistic edit cases.
rows.verification_method: Crossref API (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1145/2635868.2635929: six authors, FSE'14 proceedings, pp 654-665); OpenAlex abstract (https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1145/2635868.2635929); Semantic Scholar API cross-check.
